data.title: Mužla-Čenkov – a 3D visualisation of the hillfort
data.excerpt: A Slavic hillfort with a dominant guard and military role stood at Mužla-Čenkov on the bank of the Danube in the 9th and 10th centuries. Together with Igor Furugláš we created a visualisation of it based on two monographs by the archaeologists who excavated the site, consulting the key parts directly with Dr Milan Hanuliak.

timeline.title: The Slavic hillfort at Mužla-Čenkov
timeline.description: A Slavic hillfort with a dominant guard and military role extended over the site of Mužla-Čenkov.

children.text: A Slavic hillfort extended over the site of Mužla-Čenkov in the 9th and 10th centuries; parts of it lie in what is today the locality of Vilmakert. It can be counted among the hillforts with a dominant guard and military role. The site lies directly on the bank of the Danube, on today's border with Hungary. Thanks to its favourable position it was already occupied in prehistory, but it acquired its greatest importance in the period of the existence of Great Moravia.
THE NEW RECONSTRUCTION OF THE HILLFORT IS HERE

In cooperation with Igor Furugláš (Dwarf Art) we attempted to create an approximate picture of the hillfort in the period of its heyday. Our basis was two monographs by the archaeologists who excavated the hillfort: Hanuliak, Šalkovský, Kuzma: Mužla-Čenkov I. Osídlenie z 9. – 12. st., Nitra 1993, and Hanuliak, Kuzma: Mužla-Čenkov II: osídlenie z 9. – 13. storočia, Nitra 2015. Some key parts of the reconstruction were discussed directly with Dr Milan Hanuliak.

The visualisation seeks to give an approximate idea of how the Slavic hillfort at Mužla looked. The course of the fortification, its composition and the density of the houses follow fairly closely the evidence from the archaeologists that we had available. Besides the dwelling houses, the hillfort of course also contained countless farm buildings, storage pits, refuse pits and all manner of objects of everyday use and clutter, which made up the everyday reality of the hillfort. Modelling those was already beyond our powers, nor was it our aim.
At any rate, you now have at least this imperfect, virtual chance to walk around a hillfort of our ancestors that is 1,200 years old and to savour its atmosphere.
Our huge thanks go to Igor for his patience and for a job well done.
